terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build main.cpp and repair.cpp into one program here and run it.

tasks.title: Move the class into repair.h
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/repair.h`, move `class Repair` out of `src/main.cpp`, inside an include guard, with the `#include` this file needs for `std::string`. Keep its members, private as they were, and keep the first line of the constructor and of each function, with a semicolon in place of its body: the bodies go to `repair.cpp` in Task 2. Take the class out of `main.cpp`, which keeps `#include "repair.h"`.

Check builds a program of its own that includes `repair.h` twice before anything else, with bodies of its own for the class's functions, as `repair.cpp` will give them. It makes a repair, reads it through a `const Repair&`, tries `addMinutes`'s rule, and compiles a line of its own outside the class that reads `minutes`, which must be refused. Once the task passes otherwise, Check also looks that `main.cpp` no longer writes the class.
nextSteps: Write the guard's `#ifndef` and `#define` at the top of `repair.h`, and its `#endif` on the last line.
Add `#include <string>`, then move the class from `main.cpp`, with its `};`.
In the class, end each function's first line with a semicolon and take its body away.
Build both files with the terminal's command: the linker will say what has no body yet.
hints: A header holds what other files need to know: the class, its members and the first line of each function. The include guard stops a file that includes it twice from meeting the class twice.
Only the bodies leave. The constructor's line keeps its parameters and loses its member initialiser list, which goes with its body. `const` at the end of a getter stays.
The shape is `#ifndef REPAIR_H`, `#define REPAIR_H`, `#include <string>`, the class with lines like `int getTicket() const;` and `Repair(int number, const std::string& name);`, then `#endif`.

tasks.title: Write the member functions in repair.cpp
tasks.description:
In `src/repair.cpp`, include `repair.h` above `// Task 2`. Under `// Task 2`, write the body of the constructor and of every function the class declares, moved from `main.cpp`, each with `Repair::` in front of its name. Each first line matches its line in the class, `const` included, and the constructor keeps its member initialiser list.

Check builds a program of its own with a `repair.h` of its own, written as Task 1 asks, and links it with your `repair.cpp`. It makes repairs on memory that still holds old values, reads them back through a `const Repair&`, and tries `addMinutes`'s rule. So this task is judged on its own.
nextSteps: Write `#include "repair.h"` below the file's first comment.
Move each body from `main.cpp`, and put `Repair::` in front of each name.
The constructor becomes `Repair::Repair(...)`, with its member initialiser list after the round brackets.
Build both `.cpp` files together with the terminal's command and run the program.
hints: Outside the class, a member function's name is written with the class's name and `::` in front. Without it, it is a new function of its own, and the class's members mean nothing in it.
The first line in the `.cpp` must match the class's line: the same parameter types, the same return type and the same `const` at the end. Otherwise the compiler says it matches no declaration.
The shape is `int Repair::getTicket() const { return ticket; }` and `Repair::Repair(int number, const std::string& name) : ticket(number), item(name), minutes(0) {}`.

tasks.title: Write the bench line in main.cpp
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3` in `src/main.cpp`, write a function called `benchLine` that takes a repair as a reference to a `const Repair` and gives back its line for the bench as a `std::string`: the ticket, a space, the item, `, ` and the minutes, then ` min`. Like this:

```
3101 mantel clock, 75 min
```

`benchLine` is outside the class, so it reads the repair through its public functions. Check builds your `main.cpp` with a `repair.h` of its own in place of yours, makes repairs of its own and reads what `benchLine` gives back. The class must have left `main.cpp` (Task 1) for this to build.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `const Repair&` in, a `std::string` back.
Read the ticket, the item and the minutes through the getters.
Turn the two numbers into text with `std::to_string`, and join the parts with `+`.
Print `benchLine` of a repair from `main`, and build both files.
hints: `main.cpp` includes `repair.h`, so it knows the class and can call its public functions. The members stay private.
The repair comes in as a `const` reference, so only functions marked `const` can be called on it: the getters are.
The shape is `return std::to_string(repair.getTicket()) + " " + repair.getItem() + ", " + std::to_string(repair.getMinutes()) + " min";`.
